title: Writing linear equations
lede: Turn a graph, two points or a real situation into an equation you can use to predict, compare and decide.

sections.md:
## Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b
- **m** = slope (the rate)
- **b** = y-intercept (the starting value, where the line crosses the y-axis, when x = 0)

This is the most useful form for real life, because so many things work as **starting amount + rate × quantity**:

- Phone plan: **$30 a month + $10 per gigabyte** → y = 10x + 30
- Truck rental: **$300 + $0.90 per mile** → y = 0.9x + 300
- Savings: **$500 now + $200 a week** → y = 200x + 500

sections.title: From slope and intercept
sections.problem: A line has slope −3 and crosses the y-axis at 7.

sections.title: From two points
steps: Plug one point into y = 2x + b: 5 = 2(2) + b → b = 1.

sections.md:
## Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
When you know a **slope** and **any point** (not necessarily the intercept), this form writes the equation instantly.

Slope 4, through (3, 10): **y − 10 = 4(x − 3)**. Simplify if you like: y = 4x − 2.

## Standard form: Ax + By = C
Useful when two quantities share a total. *Tickets cost $5 for kids (x) and $12 for adults (y); you have $120*: **5x + 12y = 120**.

Intercepts are easy here: set x = 0 to get the y-intercept (12y = 120, y = 10); set y = 0 to get the x-intercept (5x = 120, x = 24).

sections.q: A gym charges a $50 sign-up fee plus $25 per month. Which equation gives total cost y after x months?
sections.why: Rate (per month) is **m = 25**; the one-time fee is the starting value **b = 50**.

sections.md:
## Parallel and perpendicular lines
- **Parallel** lines have the **same slope** (and different intercepts). They never meet.
- **Perpendicular** lines have slopes that are **negative reciprocals**: flip the fraction and change the sign. Their product is −1.

| Slope | Parallel slope | Perpendicular slope |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2 | −1/2 |
| −3/4 | −3/4 | 4/3 |
| 1 | 1 | −1 |

sections.title: Build a model and use it
sections.problem: Broker pays a flat $400 per load plus $1.50 per loaded mile. Write the equation and find the pay for a 620-mile load.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Mixing up m and b** in word problems. The rate ("per" something) is m; the one-time amount is b.
- **Point-slope sign:** y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). If the point is (−2, 5), it's y − 5 = m(x **+ 2**).
- **Perpendicular needs both changes:** flip **and** change the sign. 2 → −1/2, not 1/2.

practice.q: Line through (0, 3) and (2, 11). What's the slope?
Line through (1, 4) and (3, 10). What is b in y = mx + b?
Which line is parallel to y = 2x + 7?
Truck rental: $300 + $0.90 per mile. Cost for 450 miles?

practice.why: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) with x₁ = −2: x − (−2) = **x + 2**.
practice.hint: Subtracting a negative turns into adding.

practice.q: A line is perpendicular to y = (2/3)x − 1 and passes through (0, 4). What's its y-value at x = 6?
practice.hint: Flip 2/3 and change the sign. The point (0, 4) gives you b.

practice.q: Your account had $1,200 after week 2 and $2,000 after week 6, growing linearly. How much did you start with (week 0)?
practice.why: Slope = (2,000 − 1,200) ÷ (6 − 2) = 200 per week. Going back 2 weeks from week 2: 1,200 − 400 = **$800**.
practice.hint: Find the weekly rate, then work backward to week 0.

practice.q: Plan A: $40/month + $0.10/minute. Plan B: $0.30/minute, no monthly fee. Which equations model them (x = minutes)?
practice.why: Rate per minute is m; the monthly fee is b. Next lesson, you'll find where they cost the same.
practice.hint: Which number is per minute, and which is fixed?
